aspects.says: A compile-time constant is copied into the reading class by javac, so reading it neither initialises its class nor sees a default value.
basis: section:Static Initialisers Run in Textual Order, and a Cycle Lets Code Read a Field Before It Is Set

aspects.says: A loader defines a name once: defining it again is a LinkageError, and a custom loader can't define a java.* class.
basis: section:Each Loader Asks Its Parent First, So the JDK's Classes Always Come from the JDK's Loaders

aspects.says: Static initialisers run in textual order, and in a cycle between two classes the class used second reads the first one's field before it is set, so a final field keeps a default value that depends on which class was used first.
basis: section:Static Initialisers Run in Textual Order, and a Cycle Lets Code Read a Field Before It Is Set

aspects.says: Two threads that initialise a class cycle from both ends wait for each other forever; on Java 21 they report RUNNABLE, findDeadlockedThreads returns null, and a thread dump names the class initialization monitor.
basis: section:Two Threads That Initialise a Cycle from Both Ends Wait for Each Other Forever

aspects.says: A class is loaded when code or the verifier first needs it, and its static initialisers run only at its first use, such as new, a static method call or a non-constant static field read.
basis: section:A Class Is Loaded When Code First Needs It, and Initialised Only When Code First Uses It

aspects.says: A class is identified by its name and its defining loader, so a plugin loader that defines its own copy of the host's interface produces objects the host can't cast to it, while parent-first delegation gives both sides one class.
basis: section:A Class Is Its Name Plus the Loader That Defined It

aspects.says: ClassLoader.loadClass returns a class it already loaded, else asks its parent, and defines the class itself only when the parent can't, so the loader asked is not always the loader that defines.
basis: section:Each Loader Asks Its Parent First, So the JDK's Classes Always Come from the JDK's Loaders

aspects.says: Each thread has its own JVM stack, program counter and native method stack; the heap and the method area are shared by all threads.
basis: section:Each Thread Has Its Own Stack and Program Counter; the Heap and Method Area Are Shared
aspects.reason: where the JVM keeps a frame, a program counter or class metadata is seen through stack walks and the JVM's own errors, not through code a reader writes and a test can grade; the page ties each area to a run
